title: Caring for animals, soil and water: using them so they last

summary.text: A cow eats the same field of grass day after day, and the field stays green. Grass grows from the bottom of each leaf, close to the soil, so it grows back after grazing. Using something carefully, so that it lasts, is called conservation. Cows, buffaloes, hens, bees and silkworms give people milk, eggs, honey and silk, and each of them needs water, shade, food and kindness in return. Soil needs a cover of roots and leaves, or the rain washes it away. Water needs saving too: Indian cities now catch the rain from their roofs and send it back into the ground.
summary.art: A cow grazing a green field beside a village tank, with a honeybee on a flower, a terrace pipe pouring rain into a pit, and a small tub of cut wheat grass growing back on a city window sill.

intro.hook: A cow eats grass for about eight hours a day, often in the same field. If you cut a plant's stem, the plant usually does not grow taller from that stem again. So why does the field not run out of grass?
intro.text: In this unit you find the answer by growing wheat and moong in a tub on your window, and cutting both. You find out what the animals who help us need from us, how a cover of roots keeps soil in place, and how cities like Chennai catch the rain. You also meet a bird park where people sent the buffaloes away to protect the birds, and the birds lost out.
intro.art: A child at a city window looking at a plastic tub with tall wheat on one side and moong on the other, holding a pair of scissors and a ruler.

outcomes: I can name at least six animals that help people, say what each one gives, and say what she needs from us to stay well.
I can explain, from my own cutting test, why grass grows back after a cow eats the top, and why many other plants do not.
I can explain what overgrazing is, and why a bare field loses its soil in the rain.
I can run a fair test, measure plants with a ruler, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain what conservation means, with examples for soil, forests, animals and water.
I can describe at least four ways to save water at home, and explain how rainwater harvesting refills the ground.
I can tell the true story of the buffaloes of Keoladeo, and say what it teaches about protecting nature.

terms.meaning: Using and protecting something carefully, so that it lasts for a long time.
terms.example: Cutting only the tops of the coriander, so the plant grows more leaves next week, is conservation.
terms.art: A hand snipping the top leaves off a pot of coriander with scissors, leaving the lower stems.

terms.meaning: An animal that lives with people and is cared for by them, such as a cow, a goat, a hen or a dog.
terms.example: A Kangayam bullock that pulls a cart in Tamil Nadu is a domestic animal.
terms.art: A grey Kangayam bullock with big curved horns standing beside a wooden cart.

terms.meaning: To eat grass and other low plants growing in a field, a little at a time.
terms.example: Buffaloes graze on the grass beside a village tank.
terms.art: Two black buffaloes with their heads down, eating grass beside a pond.

terms.meaning: When too many animals eat in one place for too long, so the plants are eaten down to the ground and cannot grow back.
terms.example: A field where goats are kept all year can turn into bare, dusty ground.
terms.art: A dusty brown field with a few tufts of grass and many goats looking for food.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant where new cells are made, so the plant grows longer there. Scientists call it a meristem.
terms.example: A grass leaf's growing point is at the bottom, near the soil. A moong plant's growing point is at the tip of the stem.
terms.art: A wheat seedling and a moong seedling side by side, each with a small glowing dot: low down for the wheat, at the top for the moong.

terms.meaning: When rain or wind carries away the top layer of soil.
terms.example: After heavy rain, brown water runs off a bare slope, carrying soil with it.
terms.art: Brown muddy water running down a bare slope into a drain.

terms.meaning: Water that soaks down into the ground and fills the tiny spaces between grains of soil, sand and rock. Wells and borewells pump it up.
terms.example: Many flats in Bengaluru and Chennai get some of their water from a borewell.
terms.art: A cut-away drawing of the ground under a building, with blue water filling the gaps between sand grains and a borewell pipe reaching down.

terms.meaning: Catching rain from roofs and ground, and storing it in a tank or sending it into the ground through a pit.
terms.example: A pipe from the terrace of a Chennai building carries rain into a pit filled with stones and sand.
terms.art: Rain falling on a flat terrace, flowing down a pipe into a pit of stones and sand beside the building.

terms.meaning: To carry pollen from one flower to another, so the flower can make seeds and fruit.
terms.example: A honeybee pollinates the flowers of a mango tree while she drinks their nectar.
terms.art: A honeybee with yellow pollen on her legs on a cluster of small mango flowers.

terms.meaning: A medicine that teaches the body to fight a disease before the disease arrives.
terms.example: Pet dogs get a rabies vaccine every year, so they cannot catch or spread rabies.
terms.art: A vet giving a calm dog an injection while a girl holds the dog's lead.

terms.meaning: To lie and roll in water or mud to cool down.
terms.example: On a hot afternoon, buffaloes wallow in a pond with only their heads showing.
terms.art: Three buffaloes in a muddy pond with only their heads and backs above the water.

explanations.definition: Conservation is using and protecting something carefully, so that it lasts: soil, water, forests, animals and plants.
explanations.description: Some things grow back, like grass, trees and fish. They last for ever if we take less than grows back. Other things take thousands of years to form, like good soil and the water deep under the ground. These must be used very slowly, or they run out. Conservation means knowing how fast something comes back, and taking less than that.
examples: Picking only a few curry leaves from each branch, so the plant can grow new ones.
Fishing boats on India's east and west coasts stop fishing for some weeks each year, while many fish lay their eggs.
Planting trees on a hillside, so their roots hold the soil.
explanations.art: A curry leaf plant in a pot with a few sprigs picked and new leaves sprouting, beside a small fishing boat pulled up on a beach.
explanations.context: This card says what conservation means, with examples from Indian homes and coasts.

explanations.concept: Why grass grows back after grazing
explanations.definition: A grass leaf grows from a growing point at the bottom, close to the soil. When an animal bites off the top, the growing point is left, and the leaf keeps growing.
explanations.description: A grass plant has a hard problem: cows, goats, buffaloes, deer and grasshoppers eat them all the time. The grass answers this by keeping their growing points low, near the ground, where teeth rarely reach. So the leaf just keeps pushing up from the bottom, like toothpaste from a tube. Most other plants, like moong, beans and tomatoes, grow from the tip of each stem. Cut the tip off and that stem stops getting taller. The plant can only grow again from a bud lower down, if one is left. This is why a lawn can be cut every week, and a field can be grazed every day. Grasses and grazing animals have lived together for millions of years.
examples: In the cutting test, the cut wheat grew taller within two days. The cut moong stems stayed short stumps.
A lawn mower cuts the grass every week, and the lawn stays green.
Sugarcane, bamboo, rice and wheat are all grasses.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: a cut wheat leaf pushing up from the bottom with an arrow, and a cut moong stem with no tip left.
explanations.context: This card explains the cutting test, where you cut wheat and moong at the same height and watched what grew back.

explanations.concept: Overgrazing: when the field cannot grow back
explanations.definition: Overgrazing is when animals eat plants faster than the plants grow back, until the ground is bare.
explanations.description: Grass grows back, but only so fast. Grass plants need their leaves to catch sunlight and make food. If animals eat them again and again before they regrow, they use up the food stored in their roots. Too many hooves also trample the soil hard. Soon the roots die, the ground is bare, and the next rain washes the soil away. Herders who move their animals from field to field give each field time to grow back.
examples: In the bare tub test, rain washed far more soil out of the bare tub than out of the tub of wheat roots.
In many dry places in India, village grazing land has turned bare where too many animals are kept.
Herders in Rajasthan and Gujarat walk their sheep and camels to new places through the year.
explanations.art: A field split in two: one half green with a few cows, the other half bare and dusty with many animals crowded together.
explanations.context: This card says what happens when a field is eaten faster than the grass can grow back.

explanations.concept: Animals who help us, and what they need
explanations.definition: Useful animals give people food, work and materials. In return, they need clean water, the right food, shade, a clean shelter, rest and care when they are ill.
explanations.description: Each animal has her own needs, which come from her own body. A buffalo has dark skin and fewer sweat glands than a cow, so she heats up fast in the sun. She wallows in water or mud to cool down. So a buffalo needs a pond, a shower or a wet floor on hot days. A hen needs a dry, clean coop, because damp and dirt bring disease. A bullock that pulls a cart needs rest in the hottest hours. Honeybees need flowers without poison sprays. A silkworm caterpillar eats mulberry leaves and almost nothing else, and needs fresh ones every day. Caring for an animal starts with asking what her life is like.
examples: Cows and buffaloes give milk. Their dung is used as manure and as fuel.
Hens give eggs. Bees give honey and pollinate crops. Silkworms give silk. Sheep give wool.
Bullocks pull ploughs and carts. Dogs guard homes and help people who cannot see.
explanations.art: A row of animals with what they give: a buffalo and a steel can of milk, a hen and eggs, a bee and honey, a silkworm and a silk thread, a sheep and wool.
explanations.context: This card lists animals that help people and what each one needs in return.

explanations.concept: Caring for animals is also the law
explanations.definition: In India, the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act of 1960 makes it a crime to beat, overload, starve or neglect an animal.
explanations.description: Good care is simple to say. Give clean water every day, more in summer. Give shade and rest in the hottest hours. Keep the shed or coop clean and dry. Get vaccines, such as the rabies vaccine for dogs. Never feed animals plastic, or let them eat from rubbish. Cows that wander city streets often swallow plastic bags with food scraps inside. The bags cannot be digested and fill up their stomachs. Vets in Indian cities have taken many kilograms of plastic out of single cows.
examples: On Mattu Pongal, families in Tamil Nadu bathe their cattle, paint their horns and feed them pongal, to thank them.
Tying food waste in a bag and throwing it on the road can harm a cow. A bin with a lid keeps it away from her.
A dog bowl of fresh water in a shady spot helps street dogs in May.
explanations.art: A family in a Tamil Nadu village on Mattu Pongal, bathing a cow with painted blue and red horns and a flower garland.
explanations.context: This card says what good care for animals looks like, and what the law in India says.

explanations.definition: Soil stays in place when plants cover it. Roots hold the grains together, and leaves break the force of the rain.
explanations.description: Good soil forms very slowly, from broken rock and dead plants. A few centimetres can take hundreds of years. A raindrop hitting bare soil knocks grains loose, and the running water carries them off. Under grass or fallen leaves, the drops land softly, the water soaks in, and the roots hold the soil like a net. That is why a bare, overgrazed field or a cut forest loses its soil so fast in the monsoon.
examples: In the bare tub test, the water from the bare tub came out brown. The water from the wheat tub was much clearer.
Tea gardens in the Nilgiris are planted in rows along the slopes, to slow the water down.
Farmers leave crop stubble or grow a cover crop, so the soil is never bare.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a grassy slope with roots holding the soil, next to a bare slope with muddy water running off.
explanations.context: This card explains why soil washes away when there are no plants on it.

explanations.concept: People who stood up for forests
explanations.definition: Forests hold soil and water, give homes to animals and plants, and give people food, fuel and medicine. Many forests in India were saved by ordinary people, often women.
explanations.description: In 1983, people in Uttara Kannada, in Karnataka, hugged the trees of their forest so the loggers could not cut them. This was the Appiko movement. Appiko means 'hug' in Kannada. They followed the Chipko movement of the Himalayas. In Kerala, scientists, writers and villagers campaigned for years to save Silent Valley, a rainforest where a dam was planned. The poet Sugathakumari was one of its leaders. The dam was dropped, and Silent Valley became a national park in 1984.
examples: The lion-tailed macaque, a monkey found only in the Western Ghats, lives in Silent Valley.
Sacred groves, small forests kept by villages and temples, are found all over Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
A forest's roots and fallen leaves let rain soak into the ground and fill streams slowly.
explanations.art: Villagers in a Western Ghats forest with their arms round tall trees, and a lion-tailed macaque with a grey mane watching from a branch.
explanations.context: This card tells how people in India protected their forests.

explanations.concept: Saving water, and putting it back in the ground
explanations.definition: Water conservation means using less water, and helping rain soak back into the ground so wells and borewells refill.
explanations.description: Most Indian cities get water from rivers, lakes and reservoirs, and from the ground. When roads and buildings cover the soil, rain runs into drains and out to sea, so less soaks down to refill the groundwater. In 2003, Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings. In 2019, Chennai's main lakes went almost dry, and the city needed water from trains and tankers. Rain on a terrace can be sent down a pipe into a pit of stones and sand, and soak into the ground. At home, small habits save a lot: a mug instead of a running tap, fixing drips, and using rice-washing water for plants.
examples: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre of terrace is 1 litre of water.
Old tanks called eris in Tamil Nadu, and temple tanks across South India, catch rain and help it soak into the ground.
Water used to wash vegetables can water a potted plant.
explanations.art: A city building in the rain, with a pipe from the terrace into a pit, and blue arrows going down into the ground to a borewell.
explanations.context: This card explains how water is saved at home and how cities put rain back into the ground.

explanations.concept: Is it fair to use animals at all?
explanations.description: People in India and everywhere disagree about this, and each side has good reasons. Many families have lived with cows, goats and hens for thousands of years, and care for them well. Others think animals should not be kept to give us things. Most silk is made by boiling the cocoons with the young moth still inside, and some people will not wear it for that reason.
examples: Ahimsa silk, also called peace silk, is made after the moth has come out of the cocoon.
Some people eat no animal foods at all, and are called vegans.
Many dairy farmers in Kerala and Karnataka keep only a few cows, and know each one by name.

perspectives.explanation: My cows are part of my family. I feed them, keep them cool and call the vet when they are ill. The milk feeds my children and pays for school.
A cow's milk is made for her calf. Animals have their own lives and feelings, so we should not keep them to take from them, however kindly.
We can measure how well an animal lives: is she healthy, can she move, rest and be with others? Whatever people choose, the animal's life must go well.

explanations.art: A woman milking a cow in a Kerala shed, a calf beside them, and a silkworm cocoon on a mulberry leaf.
explanations.context: This card is about a real disagreement: whether people should keep animals for what they give.

explanations.concept: Do grazing animals help or harm a wild place?
explanations.description: It depends on the place, the animals and how many there are. Too many animals strip the land bare. But some wild places stay healthy only because something keeps the plants short. In Keoladeo National Park, in Bharatpur, buffaloes were banned in 1982, and a wetland grass spread over the shallow water.
examples: In Keoladeo, the grass Paspalum spread after the buffaloes were sent out, and park staff had to cut it back.
In grasslands, wild grazers like blackbuck and gaur keep some plants down and let others grow.
On many Indian hills, too many goats have left bare slopes.

perspectives.explanation: Village animals compete with wild animals for food and trample nests. Keep them out of protected areas.
Some places were shaped by grazing for centuries. Take the grazers away and the plants change. A small, managed number of animals can help.

explanations.art: A wetland with herons and storks on trees, and a mat of tall grass covering the shallow water where buffaloes used to graze.
explanations.context: This card is about whether grazing animals belong in protected places.

agreed.text: Grass leaves grow from a growing point near their base, so grass can be grazed or mowed again and again.
agreed.evidence: Plant scientists have mapped where the new cells are made in grass leaves. Farmers and park managers see it every time a lawn or field regrows.

agreed.text: Bare soil washes away far faster than soil covered by plants.
agreed.evidence: Measurements on farms and slopes all over the world show it. You can see it yourself in the bare tub test.

agreed.text: Most flowering crops make more fruit and seed when bees and other insects visit them.
agreed.evidence: Farmers and scientists compare crops visited by insects with crops covered by nets. The covered ones usually set less fruit.

agreed.text: Rainwater harvesting helps refill groundwater in cities.
agreed.evidence: After Tamil Nadu made it compulsory in 2003, studies in Chennai reported higher water levels in many wells over the next few years.

challenging.claim: Keeping all people and their animals out of a forest or park is always the best way to protect it.
challenging.who: An idea held by many park managers in the twentieth century
challenging.for: Fewer people and animals means less cutting, hunting and trampling.
challenging.against: At Keoladeo, the wetland grew over with grass once the buffaloes were sent out. Many forest people protect their forests well, as the women of Chipko did.
challenging.context: This card is about whether nature is protected best by keeping people out.

challenging.claim: A plant that has been eaten is damaged, and is worse off.
challenging.for: Losing leaves means less food made from sunlight.
challenging.against: Grasses grow back from the base. Some grasses even make more shoots after grazing, and grazing stops tall plants from shading them out.
challenging.context: This card is about whether being eaten always harms a plant.

challenging.claim: Saving water at home makes no difference, because farms use most of the water.
challenging.for: Farms do use most of India's water.
challenging.against: In cities, homes use most of the piped water. When Chennai's lakes dried up in 2019, every litre saved at home mattered.
challenging.context: This card is about whether saving water at home matters.

big_questions.q: Grass grows back from the bottom after a cow eats the top. Is the grass harmed, or have they simply been shared?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the grass lost, and what they still have. Did your cut wheat look unhappy?

big_questions.q: Why do you think grasses keep their growing point low, while moong keeps theirs at the top?
big_questions.hint: Who eats grass? Who eats moong? Where does each plant need to reach?

big_questions.q: A cow gives milk, and the family gives her food and care. Is that a fair trade? Who decides?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the cow would choose, if she could say.

big_questions.q: If something grows back, can we take it for ever? How would we know how much is too much?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tub you cut again and again. Did the wheat grow back the same each time?

big_questions.q: The people of Keoladeo had grazed buffaloes there for a long time. Should the park belong to the birds, the buffaloes or the people?
big_questions.hint: Is there a way for all three to share?

story.title: The Field That Never Ran Out
story.note: Made up: Kavya, Selvi Athai, Arun and their farm are invented. True: Kangayam cattle come from the Kangayam area of Tiruppur district in Tamil Nadu. On Mattu Pongal, the day after Thai Pongal, families bathe their cattle, paint their horns, put garlands on them and feed them pongal. Grass grows from the base of the leaf, and goats often eat plants down to the ground. Buffaloes wallow because they heat up fast.
text: Kavya lived on the sixth floor of a building in Velachery, in Chennai. The only plants she knew were the tulsi and the money plant on the balcony. So when her family went to Selvi Athai's farm near Kangayam for Pongal, she did not know what to expect.

Athai's farm had four Kangayam cows, grey and white, with big curved horns. It had two black buffaloes, a few goats, and hens that ran everywhere. Behind the cow shed was a wide field of grass, with a small pond at one end.

On the first morning, Kavya watched Athai walk the cows out to the field. They put their heads down and began to eat. They tore off the grass with a jerk of the head, chewing and moving on, chewing and moving on.
"How long will they eat?" Kavya asked.
"Most of the day," said Athai. "A cow eats for hours and hours. Then she lies down and chews it all again."

The next morning, the cows went to the same field. And the next. Kavya began to worry. At home, when Amma cut coriander for rasam, the bunch was gone. "Athai, the cows eat this field every day. When will it be finished?"

Athai laughed. "Come and see." She knelt down at the edge of the field, where the cows had eaten the day before. The grass was short there, cut off flat, as if with scissors. "Look at the tips of these leaves."
Kavya looked. The leaves had flat, chewed ends. But they were not as short as she expected.

"Yesterday these were bitten right down," said Athai. "Today they are a little taller. Grass grows from the bottom of the leaf, not the top. The cow bites off the top, and the bottom keeps pushing up."
Kavya thought about this. "So the cow never eats the part that grows?"
"Not if she just eats the top. That is why a field can feed cows for a hundred years."
Just then, Kavya's cousin Arun came running. He was six, and he loved the goats. "Athai! The goats got into your bhindi plants!"

They ran to the vegetable patch behind the house. Two goats were eating happily. The bhindi plants had been bitten off at the top, and some were chewed right down to the soil. Athai shooed the goats away and tied them up.
"Will the bhindi grow back too?" asked Arun.

Athai shook her head slowly. "Not like grass. A bhindi plant grows from the tip of their stem. The goats ate the tips. A few may grow a new shoot from lower down. The ones chewed to the ground are finished."
Arun looked sad. Kavya put her arm round him. "It isn't the goats' fault," she said. "They don't know which plants grow from the bottom."

"Goats eat almost anything," said Athai. "That is why we keep them tied, and move them to a new place every few days. If they stay too long in one place, they pull the plants up by the roots. Then nothing grows back. The rain washes the bare soil away, and it takes hundreds of years to make more."
That afternoon it was hot, even in January. The buffaloes walked down to the pond and lay in the water, with only their heads and their backs showing. Kavya laughed. "They're having a bath!"

"They're keeping cool," said Athai. "A buffalo has dark skin and not many sweat glands, so she gets hot fast. If there were no pond, I would have to pour water on them. Every animal on this farm needs something different. The hens need a dry coop. The cows need clean water three or four times a day. The buffaloes need their pond."
"And the pond needs the rain," said Kavya.
Athai smiled. "That is right. We dug the pond deeper three years ago. Now the rain from the whole field runs into it, and soaks down slowly. My well has water even in May."

The next day was Mattu Pongal. Kavya and Arun helped Athai bathe the cows. They painted their horns blue and red, and put garlands of marigolds round their necks. They fed them sweet pongal from their hands. Kavya stroked the oldest cow's nose. "Thank you for the milk," she said.

Before they left, Kavya pulled up a few blades of grass from the field edge, very carefully, with the roots. She wanted to see the bottom of a grass leaf for herself. In the car, she held them up to the window. At the bottom of each leaf, near the roots, the grass was pale and soft, tucked inside the leaf below.
"That is where they grow," Kavya told Arun. "Right at the bottom, where the cows can't reach."
Back in Chennai, Kavya asked Amma for a handful of wheat and a tub of soil. She wanted to see a field grow back on her own balcony.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya worries that the cows will finish the field, because when you cut most plants, that part is gone. But grass grows from the bottom of each leaf, near the soil, so a cow that eats only the top leaves the growing part behind. The goats show the other side: plants that grow from the tip, like bhindi, do not grow back the same way, and animals kept too long in one place eat plants to the roots. Caring for a farm means knowing what each living thing needs, from the buffalo's pond to the grass's time to regrow.
ask: Why didn't the cows run out of grass, even though they ate the same field every day?
Why did Athai keep the goats tied and move them every few days?
What did each animal on the farm need from Athai?
Kavya said it wasn't the goats' fault. Do you agree? What could Athai do so the goats and the vegetables both do well?

experiments.title: The Cutting Test: what grows back, wheat or moong?
experiments.context: In this experiment you grow wheat and moong side by side in one tub of soil. When both are tall, you cut them at the same height, like a cow grazing. Then you watch for four days to see which one grows back.
experiments.question: If we cut wheat and moong at the same height, which one grows back?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will cut the wheat and the moong 2 centimetres above the soil. After four days, which will be taller: the wheat, the moong, or both the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Grow both in the same tub, with the same soil, the same water and the same light. Cut both at exactly 2 centimetres. Only the kind of plant is different. Measure 3 plants of each kind, not 1, because one plant might be odd. Leave 5 wheat plants uncut, to compare.

materials.item: 4 tablespoons of whole wheat grains (gehu). Whole jowar or bajra also work.
2 tablespoons of whole green moong
2 plastic tubs or old ice-cream boxes, each about 15 centimetres across and 8 centimetres deep, with 4 small holes poked in the bottom
soil from a potted plant, or a small bag of potting soil, enough to fill both tubs
2 old plates to stand the tubs on
a ruler with centimetres
scissors
2 small bowls for soaking, and a cup for watering
an ice-cream stick or a strip of card, and a pen, for labels

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the tub. Wash your hands after touching soil. Don't eat the soaked grains.

schedule.what: Soak the wheat and the moong overnight, in separate bowls.
Fill the tub with soil. Sow wheat on one half and moong on the other. Cover lightly and water. Sow a second tub with only wheat, for the Bare Tub Test.
Water if the soil feels dry. Look for shoots.
Water and look.
Water and look. Measure the tallest plant of each kind.
Both should be about 8 to 12 centimetres tall. Measure 3 of each. Guess. Cut both at 2 centimetres, leaving 5 wheat uncut.
Measure the 3 cut wheat and the 3 cut moong.
Measure again. Look closely at the tips of the cut wheat.
Measure for the last time. Say what you think, what you saw and why. Keep the tub for the next experiments.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each time. On the last day, draw one cut wheat plant and one cut moong plant, side by side, with their heights.
