flow.context: This is the first step of the Cutting Test. You soak the seeds so they start to grow.
flow.do: 1. Put 2 tablespoons of wheat in one bowl and 2 tablespoons of moong in the other. 2. Cover each with water. 3. Leave them overnight.
flow.say: A cow eats the same field every day, and the field doesn't run out. Today we start a tiny field of our own, to find out why.
flow.kid: Put wheat in one bowl. Put moong in the other. Cover them with water. Leave them till tomorrow.
flow.parent: Soaking makes the seeds swell and start growing faster. Any whole wheat from a grocery shop works, but not atta or broken wheat (dalia).

flow.context: This is the sowing step of the Cutting Test. You plant the soaked seeds in one tub.
flow.do: 1. Fill the tub with soil to about 2 centimetres from the top. 2. Put a label W on the left half and M on the right half. 3. Spread the wheat thickly over the W half. 4. Spread the moong over the M half, about a finger-width apart. 5. Cover with a thin layer of soil. 6. Water gently until the soil is damp, not muddy. 7. Put the tub on its plate by a bright window. 8. Fill the second tub the same way and spread wheat over all of it. Keep it next to the first. You will need it for the Bare Tub Test.
flow.say: We grow both in the same tub, so they get the same soil, water and light. Then the only difference is the kind of plant.
flow.kid: Fill the tub with soil. Wheat goes on one side. Moong goes on the other. Cover them with a little soil. Water gently. Now sow a second tub with only wheat.
flow.parent: A grown-up pokes the drainage holes with a heated skewer or the tip of a scissor. Wheat is a grass. Moong is not. Don't tell your child that yet.

flow.context: These are the watering days of the Cutting Test, while the plants grow.
flow.do: Every day or two, touch the soil. If it feels dry, add half a cup of water. On day 7, measure the tallest plant of each kind from the soil to the tip.
flow.say: Feel the soil first. We only water when it feels dry, because soggy soil rots seeds.
flow.kid: Touch the soil. Dry? Give half a cup of water. Wet? Leave it.
flow.wait: Water every day or two for about a week, until both kinds are 8 to 12 centimetres tall.
flow.parent: Wheat shoots usually show in 2 to 3 days and moong in 2 days. In about a week, both are usually 8 to 12 centimetres tall. In a cold room it may take 10 days. Moong grown indoors can lean towards the window, which is fine.

flow.context: This is the measuring day of the Cutting Test, just before the cut.
flow.do: 1. Choose 3 wheat plants and 3 moong plants near the middle of each half. 2. Measure each from the soil to the top. 3. Write the heights in the table as Day 9, before the cut. 4. Look closely at where each plant's leaves come from.
flow.say: Let's measure first, so we can compare later. Now look at the wheat leaves. Where do they come out of the plant? And where do the moong leaves come out?
flow.kid: Measure 3 wheat and 3 moong. Write the numbers down. Where do the wheat leaves start? Where do the moong leaves start?

ask.q: Where do the leaves come from on each plant?
good: The wheat leaves come straight out of the soil.
The moong leaves are at the top of a stem.
The moong has two round leaves and a stem.

flow.context: This is the guessing step of the Cutting Test. You guess before you cut.
flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to give a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We are going to cut both kinds at 2 centimetres, like a cow biting off the top. In four days, which will be taller? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will cut both at 2 centimetres. Which will grow back? Why do you think so? Write your guess.
flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Many children think neither will grow back, or that both will. Don't correct the guess. The test will answer it.

flow.context: This is the cutting step of the Cutting Test, where you graze your tiny field.
flow.do: 1. Stand the ruler upright in the soil. 2. Cut the 3 measured wheat plants, and all the other wheat except 5, exactly at the 2 centimetre mark. 3. Cut all the moong at 2 centimetres too. 4. Leave the 5 uncut wheat plants in one corner.
flow.say: Now we are the cow. Cut straight across, at the 2 centimetre mark, for both kinds.
flow.kid: Hold the ruler up. Cut the wheat at 2 centimetres. Cut the moong at 2 centimetres too. Leave 5 wheat plants uncut.
flow.parent: Help with the scissors. Moong seed leaves are the two thick, round leaves. If they sit lower than 2 centimetres, cut just below them, so no leaves are left on the stump. Write down which you did.

flow.context: These are the days after the cut, in the Cutting Test. You measure what grows back.
flow.do: On days 10, 11 and 13, measure the same 3 wheat and 3 moong from the soil to the top. Write each height in the table. Look at the tips of the cut wheat leaves.
flow.say: Let's measure the same plants. Look at the tips of the wheat. Are they pointed, or flat where we cut them?
flow.kid: Measure the same 3 wheat and 3 moong. Write the numbers. Look at the tips of the wheat. Pointed or flat?

check.q: The cut wheat leaves are taller, but their tips are still flat where you cut them. Where did the new part grow?
options: At the top, above the cut
At the bottom, near the soil, pushing the flat tip up
The leaf did not grow. The soil sank.
check.why: If the leaf grew at the top, the tip would be pointed and new. It is still flat, so the new part was added at the bottom and pushed the cut tip up. Picking 'at the top' is a natural guess, because many plants grow from their tips. The soil sinking a little can happen, but not by several centimetres.

flow.parent: Cut wheat usually grows back 1 to 2 centimetres a day in a warm room. New, pointed leaves also come up from the middle. The moong stumps usually stay the same height and may dry up. If a moong stump kept their round seed leaves, a small side shoot may slowly grow beside them, from a bud. Write it down if you see it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Cutting Test. You say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Make a bar for each plant on the last day. 2. Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: wheat grows back after cutting and moong doesn't. What I saw: the cut wheat grew from 2 to 7 centimetres in four days, and the moong stayed at 2. Why: wheat grows from the bottom of the leaf, so cutting the top doesn't stop them. Now read the card 'Why grass grows back after grazing'. Keep the tub for the Dot Test and the Bare Tub Test.

experiments.title: The Dot Test: does a wheat leaf grow at the top or the bottom?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put two ink dots on an uncut wheat leaf, and measure them for two days. The dots show which part of the leaf is growing.
experiments.question: Does a wheat leaf grow longer at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You put one dot 2 centimetres above the soil and one 4 centimetres above the soil. In two days, will the dots move apart, stay the same, or both move up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Mark 3 leaves, not 1, in case one leaf is odd. Measure from the same place, the top of the soil, every time.

materials.item: the 5 uncut wheat plants from the Cutting Test, or any young wheat or grass
a felt-tip pen or a sketch pen
a ruler with centimetres

experiments.safety: Press the pen gently, so the leaf doesn't tear.

schedule.what: Put two dots on 3 young leaves. Measure. Guess.
Measure again. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw one leaf on day 1 and on day 3, with its dots.

setup.art: A child's hand holding a ruler upright beside a young wheat leaf, putting a small dot on the leaf at 2 centimetres and another at 4 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Put dots at 2 and 4 centimetres above the soil.

setup.art: The same leaf two days later, taller, with both dots higher above the soil but still the same distance apart.
setup.caption: 2. Two days later, measure again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Dot Test. You mark young wheat leaves with dots.
flow.do: 1. Choose 3 young wheat leaves. 2. Hold the ruler upright in the soil beside each leaf. 3. Put a small dot on the leaf at 2 centimetres, and another at 4 centimetres. 4. Write down the heights and the gap, which is 2 centimetres.
flow.say: If a leaf grows at the top, the dots stay where they are. If the leaf grows in the middle, the dots move apart. What if she grows at the bottom? What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Put a dot at 2 centimetres. Put another at 4 centimetres. Do it on 3 leaves. What will the dots do?

flow.context: This is the last step of the Dot Test. You measure the dots again.
flow.do: 1. Measure from the soil to the lower dot on each leaf. 2. Measure the gap between the two dots. 3. Write them in the table.
flow.say: Are the dots further apart? Are they higher? What does that tell us about where the leaf grows?
flow.kid: Measure the soil to the lower dot. Measure the gap. Did the dots move apart, or just move up?

check.q: Both dots are higher above the soil, but the gap between them is still 2 centimetres. Where is the leaf growing?
options: Below the lower dot, near the soil
check.why: The gap did not change, so the part between the dots did not grow. The whole marked part moved up, so new leaf was added underneath, near the soil. If the tip were growing, the dots would not move up at all.

flow.parent: The lower dot usually rises by 1 to 3 centimetres in two days while the gap stays about the same. If the lower dot was very close to the soil, the gap may grow a little, because the growing part is just there. That is a useful clue too.

experiments.title: The Bare Tub Test: does a mat of roots keep soil from washing away?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour 'rain' on two tilted tubs of soil. One is bare. One is your second wheat tub from the Cutting Test, full of roots. You compare the water that runs off.
experiments.question: When rain falls on a slope, does a mat of grass roots stop the soil washing away?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which tub will lose more soil when we pour water on it: the bare tub or the wheat tub? What will the water look like? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same kind of soil in both tubs. Tilt them on the same books, to the same slope. Pour the same amount of water, from the same height, at the same speed. Only the cover is different.
results_table: Colour of the water that ran off
Soil settled in the bowl after 10 minutes (a little, some, a lot)

materials.item: the second tub from the Cutting Test, sown all over with wheat, 2 or more weeks old and never cut
a second tub the same size, filled with the same soil, with nothing growing
2 or 3 thick books, and a plastic bag to cover them
2 steel bowls or clear glass jars, to catch the runoff
a plastic bottle with 8 to 10 small holes in the cap, to make rain
2 cups of water for each tub

experiments.safety: Do this in the bathroom or on the balcony, where mud can be washed away. A grown-up makes the holes in the bottle cap. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Tilt both tubs. Rain on each. Compare the water and the soil that settles.

experiments.record: Draw the two bowls, colouring the water as it looked. Fill in the table.

setup.art: Two tubs of soil tilted side by side on books covered in plastic, in a bathroom, one bare and one full of thick young wheat, with a steel bowl below the low end of each.
setup.caption: 1. Tilt both tubs the same way, with a bowl below each.

setup.art: A child squeezing a bottle with a holed cap so water sprinkles like rain onto the bare tub.
setup.caption: 2. Rain 2 cups of water on each tub.

setup.art: Two glass jars side by side: one with brown muddy water and a layer of soil at the bottom, the other with much clearer water.
setup.caption: 3. Compare the water, and the soil that settles.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Bare Tub Test. You set up two tubs as slopes.
flow.do: 1. Cover the books with the plastic bag. 2. Lean both tubs on the books, at the same slope, with the holes facing down the slope. 3. Put a bowl at the low end of each tub, under the holes and the edge.
flow.say: These two tubs are two little hillsides. One is bare, like a field eaten to the ground. One is covered in grass, like a field grazed just a little.
flow.kid: Lean both tubs on the books. Same slope for both. Put a bowl under each one.
flow.parent: Soil can slide out of the bare tub. A slope of about one book height is enough. The tubs drain through the holes and over the low edge, so place the bowls to catch both.

flow.context: This is the guessing step of the Bare Tub Test.
flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before any water is poured.
flow.say: We will rain the same water on both. Which bowl will get more soil? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which bowl will get more soil? Why do you think so?

flow.context: This is the rain step of the Bare Tub Test.
flow.do: 1. Fill the bottle with 2 cups of water. 2. Hold it about 20 centimetres above the top of the bare tub. 3. Squeeze gently so it sprinkles, for about 1 minute. 4. Do the same for the wheat tub.
flow.say: Rain gently, from the same height, for the same time. Watch where the water goes.
flow.kid: Hold the bottle up high. Squeeze gently, like rain. Count to 60. Now do the other tub.
flow.parent: If water pours straight out of the bare tub without sinking in, that is part of the result too. Bare soil often forms a crust that rain runs off.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bare Tub Test. You compare the runoff.
flow.do: 1. Compare the colour of the water in the two bowls. 2. Wait 10 minutes for the soil to settle. 3. Tip the bowls gently and look at the soil at the bottom.
flow.say: Which bowl is muddier? Which has more soil at the bottom? What did the roots do?
flow.kid: Which water is browner? Wait 10 minutes. Which bowl has more soil at the bottom?

check.q: The bare tub's water was brown, and the wheat tub's water was much clearer. Why?
options: The wheat drank all the water
The roots held the soil, and the leaves slowed the drops
The wheat tub had less soil
check.why: Roots grip the soil grains, and the leaves break the force of each drop, so less soil is knocked loose. The wheat did drink some water, but not 2 cups in a minute. Both tubs had the same soil, so that was not the difference.

flow.parent: The bare tub usually gives brown water and a clear layer of soil in the bowl. The wheat tub's water is usually much clearer, because the roots form a mat. Link it to the card 'Soil needs a cover': this is why an overgrazed field loses its soil.

games.title: Four Fields: keep the herd fed without a bare field
games.context: This is a board game that everyone plays together, as one team of herders. You move one herd of cows between four fields. The grass grows back each round, but a field eaten to nothing turns bare and is lost.

printables.title: A board with four fields in a square, and a round counter from 1 to 10
items: Field 1: by the tank
Field 2: by the coconut trees
Field 3: by the temple
Field 4: by the road
A row of boxes marked Round 1 to Round 10

printables.title: 20 grass tokens and 1 herd token
items: 20 grass tokens: dried rajma, small buttons or torn green paper
1 herd token: a coin or a bottle cap

printables.title: 16 question cards to cut out
items: Where does a grass leaf grow from: the top or the bottom? (The bottom, near the soil)
Why does a moong stem stop growing taller when you cut the tip? (Moong grows from the tip of the stem)
What is overgrazing? (Animals eating plants faster than they grow back)
What holds soil in place when it rains? (Plant roots, and leaves that soften the drops)
Why does a buffalo lie in a pond on a hot day? (To cool down. She has dark skin and few sweat glands)
What does a silkworm eat? (Mulberry leaves)
Name one thing bees do for crops. (They pollinate the flowers, so the crops make fruit and seed)
Why is a plastic bag of food scraps on the road dangerous for a cow? (She can swallow the plastic, and it stays in her stomach)
What is conservation? (Using something carefully, so that it lasts)
What is groundwater? (Water that soaks into the ground and fills the gaps between soil and rock)
1 millimetre of rain falls on 1 square metre of roof. How much water is that? (1 litre)
Name one way to save water while brushing your teeth. (Use a mug, or close the tap)
Which state made rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings in 2003? (Tamil Nadu)
Appiko means 'hug' in which language? (Kannada)
What happened at Keoladeo when the buffaloes were sent out? (A wetland grass spread over the water)
Name an Indian law that protects animals from cruelty. (The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960)

rules: Put 5 grass tokens on each field. Put the herd on Field 1. Put a marker on Round 1.
Each round, the herd eats 2 grass tokens from the field they are on. Take them off the board.
Then every field that still has at least 1 token grows 1 token back. No field can hold more than 5.
A field with 0 tokens is bare. A bare field never grows back in this game, because the rain has washed its soil away.
Before the next round, you may move the herd to another field. To move, read a question card and answer it. Right answer: move. Wrong answer: the herd stays where they are.
If the herd is on a field with fewer than 2 tokens, they eat what is there and go hungry for the rest.
The team wins if the herd never goes hungry and no field turns bare for 10 rounds. Playing alone works the same way.

setup.art: A paper board with four fields drawn in a square, each with 5 dried rajma beans, and a coin on Field 1.
setup.caption: 1. Put 5 grass tokens on each field and the herd on Field 1.

setup.art: A child taking 2 beans off the field where the coin sits, then adding 1 bean to each of the other fields.
setup.caption: 2. The herd eats 2. Every field that is not bare grows 1 back.

setup.art: A child reading a question card aloud, then moving the coin to a field full of beans.
setup.caption: 3. Answer a card to move the herd.

flow.context: This is the first step of Four Fields. You set up the board and the tokens.
flow.do: 1. Draw or print the board. 2. Put 5 tokens on each field. 3. Put the herd on Field 1. 4. Shuffle the question cards.
flow.say: We are herders, all on one team. Our cows must eat every day for 10 rounds. Grass grows back, but a bare field is lost.
flow.kid: Put 5 beans on each field. Put the coin on Field 1. The coin is your herd of cows.

flow.context: This is a trial round of Four Fields, to see what happens if the herd never moves.
flow.do: Play 3 rounds with the herd staying on Field 1. Count the tokens on Field 1 after each round.
flow.say: Let's first try staying in one field. Eat 2, grow 1. What happens to Field 1?
flow.kid: Keep the herd on Field 1. Eat 2 beans. Grow 1 back. Do it 3 times. What happens?

check.q: Field 1 started with 5 tokens. Each round the herd eats 2 and the field grows 1 back. How many are left after 3 rounds?
check.why: Each round the field loses 2 and gains 1, so it loses 1 overall. After 3 rounds it has 5 take away 3, which is 2. One more round and it is close to bare. That is overgrazing.

flow.parent: Reset the board after the trial. The point is to see that a field shrinks when the herd eats faster than the grass grows back.

flow.context: This is the main game of Four Fields. You play 10 rounds and move the herd to keep every field alive.
flow.do: Play 10 rounds by the rules. Before each move, the player reads a question card and answers it.
flow.say: Where should the herd go next? Which field has had the longest rest?
flow.kid: Play 10 rounds. Answer a card to move. Try to keep every field green.
flow.parent: Moving every round or two keeps all four fields alive. A wrong answer keeps the herd in place, which makes the game harder. That is fine. Talk about which field to choose.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Fields. You talk about what kept the fields alive.
flow.do: Ask what kept the fields growing.
flow.say: What did we do that kept the fields alive? Real herders in Rajasthan move their sheep and camels across the year for the same reason.
flow.kid: What kept your fields alive? Why did moving the herd help?

ask.q: Why did moving the herd help?
good: Each field got time to grow back.
The herd ate less than grew back in each field.
No field was eaten down to nothing.

games.title: Who Needs What: a matching game of animals and their care
games.context: This is a memory game with pairs of cards. One card shows an animal who helps people. The other shows what that animal needs. You turn cards over to find the pairs.

printables.title: 16 cards: 8 animal cards and 8 need cards
items: Buffalo (gives milk) | A pond, a shower or a wet floor on hot days, because she heats up fast
Hen (gives eggs) | A dry, clean coop, because damp and dirt bring disease
Silkworm (gives silk) | Fresh mulberry leaves every day
Honeybee (gives honey and pollinates crops) | Flowers that have not been sprayed with poison
Bullock (pulls a cart or plough) | Rest and water in the hottest hours
Dog (guards the home) | A rabies vaccine every year
Cow (gives milk) | Clean food, and never plastic bags from the road
Sheep (gives wool) | A haircut, called shearing, so her wool does not get too thick and hot

rules: Cut the 16 cards and lay them face down in 4 rows.
Turn over 2 cards. If they are an animal and her need, say why she needs this, and keep the pair.
If they don't match, turn them back. The next player has a turn.
Playing alone: count how many turns you take to find all 8 pairs. Next time, try to beat it.

setup.art: 16 small cards face down in 4 rows on a mat, with a few turned up showing a hen and a dry coop.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 16 cards face down.

setup.art: A child holding up a buffalo card and a pond card together, smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Find an animal and her need, and say why.

flow.context: This is the first step of Who Needs What. You make and lay out the cards.
flow.do: 1. Write or print the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.
flow.say: Each animal who helps us has her own needs. Let's find which need goes with which animal.
flow.kid: Mix the cards. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 4.

flow.context: This is the main game of Who Needs What. You turn over cards to find the pairs.
flow.do: Take turns turning over 2 cards. A pair counts only if the player says why the animal needs this.
flow.say: You found the buffalo and the pond. Why does she need a pond?
flow.kid: Turn over 2 cards. Is it an animal and her need? Say why she needs this.
flow.parent: The reason matters more than the match. A buffalo has dark skin and few sweat glands, so she wallows to cool down. Sheep of wool breeds need shearing once or twice a year.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Needs What.
flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which need surprised you the most?
flow.kid: Which need surprised you? Answer the question.

check.q: Why does a hen need a dry coop?
options: Hens cannot walk on wet ground
check.why: Germs and tiny pests grow fast in damp, dirty bedding, and hens fall ill. Hens can walk on wet ground, and eggs do not melt. Caring for an animal starts with knowing what makes her ill.

activities.title: The Onion Test: where does a cut leaf grow from?
activities.context: In this short activity you cut the green leaves off a spring onion and stand the white root end in water. In two or three days you see where the new green comes from.

materials.item: 2 spring onions with their white bulbs and roots, from the vegetable shop
a small glass or steel tumbler with a little water
a knife, used by a grown-up, and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts with the knife.

schedule.what: Cut the green leaves 3 centimetres above the white part. Stand the bottoms in 2 centimetres of water.
Look and measure. Where did the new green come from?

activities.record: Draw the onion on day 1 and on day 3, with the heights.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting the green leaves off two spring onions on a chopping board, 3 centimetres above the white part.
setup.caption: 1. Cut the leaves 3 centimetres above the white part.

setup.art: Two spring onion bottoms standing in a steel tumbler with a little water, and new green shoots coming from the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Stand them in water and look again in two days.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Onion Test. You cut the leaves and stand the onions in water.
flow.do: 1. Cut the green leaves 3 centimetres above the white part. 2. Stand the bottoms, roots down, in 2 centimetres of water. 3. Put the tumbler by a window.
flow.say: We cut off almost all the leaves. Will the onion grow new ones? If so, where from: the top of the cut, or the middle?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the leaves. Put the white bottoms in water. Where will new green come from?

flow.context: This is the last step of the Onion Test. You look at where the new green grew.
flow.do: 1. Measure the tallest new leaf. 2. Look at where it comes out: from the cut edge, or from inside the middle.
flow.say: Where did the new leaf come from? Is the old cut edge any taller?
flow.kid: Measure the new green. Where did it come from? The cut edge, or the middle?
flow.wait: Leave the onions for 2 days. Change the water if it smells.

check.q: The new green leaves pushed up from the middle of the onion. What does this show?
options: Onions grow from the cut tips
Onion leaves grow from low down, near the bottom
check.why: Like grass, an onion makes new leaf from low down, inside the bottom of the plant. The cut edges stay where they were. Onions and grasses are both plants whose leaves grow from the base.

flow.parent: New green usually shows within 2 or 3 days in a warm room, often 2 to 5 centimetres. This links to the Cutting Test: wheat also grows from the bottom of the leaf. Once grown, the onion leaves can go into the upma.

activities.title: The Drip Count: how much water does a dripping tap waste?
activities.context: In this activity you catch the water from a dripping tap for 10 minutes. Then you work out how much it would waste in a whole day.

materials.item: a tap, opened just enough to drip about once a second
a steel tumbler or a cup
a measuring cup or a medicine cup with millilitre marks
a clock or phone timer

activities.safety: Use the caught water to water a plant afterwards, so none is wasted.

schedule.what: Catch the drips for 10 minutes. Measure. Work out a whole day.

activities.record: Write: drips in 10 minutes, millilitres in 10 minutes, and millilitres in a day.

setup.art: A tap dripping slowly into a steel tumbler on a kitchen counter, with a phone timer beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Catch the drips for 10 minutes.

setup.art: A child pouring the water from the tumbler into a measuring cup with millilitre marks.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the water in millilitres.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Drip Count. You catch drips for 10 minutes.
flow.do: 1. Open a tap until it drips about once a second. 2. Put the tumbler under it. 3. Start a 10 minute timer. 4. Count the drips in the first minute.
flow.say: One drip looks like nothing. Let's guess first. How much will we catch in 10 minutes? A spoonful, a cup or a bucket? Why?
flow.kid: Put the tumbler under the drip. Count the drips in one minute. Wait 10 minutes.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Drip Count. You measure and work out a whole day.
flow.do: 1. Pour the water into the measuring cup. 2. Write the millilitres. 3. Multiply by 6 for an hour, then by 24 for a day.
flow.say: 10 minutes, 6 times, is an hour. An hour, 24 times, is a day. How much is that?
flow.kid: Measure the water. Times 6 is one hour. Times 24 is one day.
flow.parent: One drip a second often gives about 30 to 50 millilitres in 10 minutes. That is about 4 to 7 litres a day, a full bucket every few days. A tap washer costs a few rupees.

activities.title: Rain Gauge: how much rain falls on our home?
activities.context: In this activity you make a simple rain gauge from a bottle, and use it to find out how much water falls on your balcony or terrace in one rain.

materials.item: a plastic bottle with straight sides, with the top cut off by a grown-up
a ruler with millimetres, or a paper strip marked in millimetres and taped to the bottle
a few small stones or marbles to keep the bottle from tipping
a measuring tape, to measure the balcony

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Put the gauge where a child can reach it safely, never on a ledge or parapet.

schedule.what: Make the gauge and put it in an open spot on the balcony or terrace.
After a rain, read the millimetres. Work out the litres that fell on your balcony.

activities.record: Write the date, the millimetres of rain, the balcony size and the litres.

setup.art: A plastic bottle with its top cut off, a millimetre strip taped up its side, standing on an open balcony floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put the gauge in the open, away from walls.

setup.art: A child reading the water level against the millimetre strip after rain.
setup.caption: 2. Read the millimetres after the rain.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rain Gauge. You make it and put it outside.
flow.do: 1. Put a few stones in the bottom of the bottle. 2. Add water just to cover them, and mark that level as zero. 3. Tape a millimetre strip upwards from the zero mark. 4. Put it in the open, away from walls and roofs.
flow.say: Rain falls evenly, so the depth in our bottle is the depth all over the balcony.
flow.kid: Put stones in the bottle. Add water to cover them. Mark zero there. Put it outside.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rain Gauge. You read the rain and work out the litres.
flow.do: 1. Read how many millimetres the water rose. 2. Measure the balcony's length and width in metres. 3. Multiply them for the square metres. 4. Multiply by the millimetres. That is the litres.
flow.say: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre is 1 litre. So how many litres fell on our balcony?
flow.kid: Read the millimetres. Measure the balcony. Square metres times millimetres is litres.
flow.wait: Wait for a rainy day. Check the gauge the morning after.
flow.parent: If it doesn't rain this week, use a city number instead: Chennai gets about 1,400 millimetres of rain in a year, so 1 square metre catches about 1,400 litres a year. A 3 metre by 2 metre balcony is 6 square metres.

activities.title: Thank-You Shelf: which animals helped make our home?
activities.context: In this activity you hunt around your home for things that came from animals. For each one, you name the animal and one thing she needs to live well.

materials.item: things from the kitchen and cupboard, such as milk, curd, ghee, eggs, honey, a silk saree or a woollen shawl
paper and crayons

activities.safety: Handle silk and honey jars carefully.

schedule.what: Find 5 things from animals. Draw each with her animal and one need.

activities.record: A chart with three columns: the thing, the animal, and what she needs.

setup.art: A kitchen counter with a steel can of milk, a jar of honey, an egg tray, a ghee tin and a folded silk saree.
setup.caption: 1. Gather things that came from animals.

setup.art: A child's chart with drawings: honey and a bee with a flower, milk and a cow with a water trough.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each thing with her animal and one need.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Thank-You Shelf. You find things that came from animals.
flow.do: Help your child find 5 things in the home that came from an animal.
flow.say: Milk, ghee and curd came from a cow or a buffalo. What else came from an animal?
flow.kid: Find 5 things that came from an animal. Look in the kitchen and the cupboard.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Thank-You Shelf. You name what each animal needs.
flow.do: For each thing, draw the animal and write one thing she needs.
flow.say: The honey came from bees. What do bees need to make it?
flow.kid: Draw each animal. Write one thing she needs.

good: A safe place for the hive.

flow.parent: Honeybees make honey from nectar they collect from flowers. Pesticide sprays harm them, so flowers grown without sprays matter.

projects.title: The Grazing Diary: how often can wheat be cut?
projects.context: In this project you keep cutting the wheat from the Cutting Test, every 3 days, for two weeks. You measure the regrowth each time. You find out whether grass that is grazed again and again keeps growing back as fast.

materials.item: the Cutting Test tub, with its cut wheat
a ruler and scissors
a notebook

schedule.what: Choose 3 wheat plants. Cut them at 2 centimetres. Cut 3 others at 1 centimetre. Mark both groups.
Measure all 6. Cut them again at the same heights.
Measure and cut again.
Measure and cut again.
Measure and cut again.
Measure for the last time. Make a bar chart of each cut. Say what you found.

projects.record: A table: date, regrowth of each plant since the last cut. Then a bar chart.

setup.art: A tub of wheat with two groups of plants marked by ice-cream sticks labelled 2 cm and 1 cm.
setup.caption: 1. Mark 3 plants for 2 centimetre cuts and 3 for 1 centimetre cuts.

setup.art: A child's notebook with a bar chart: the bars for each cut getting shorter over two weeks.
setup.caption: 2. Measure, cut again, and chart the regrowth.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Grazing Diary. You choose and cut the plants.
flow.do: 1. Choose 6 wheat plants. 2. Mark 3 with a stick labelled 2 cm, and 3 with a stick labelled 1 cm. 3. Cut each group at its height.
flow.say: A gentle cow takes the top. A hungry one bites close to the ground. Which plants will grow back best? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark 3 plants for 2 centimetres. Mark 3 for 1 centimetre. Cut them. Which will grow back best?

flow.context: These are the cutting days of the Grazing Diary, every 3 days.
flow.do: Every 3 days, measure how much each plant grew since the last cut. Write it down. Then cut again at the same height.
flow.say: How much did each plant grow since the last cut? More or less than last time?
flow.kid: Measure how much each one grew. Write it. Cut again.
flow.wait: Come back every 3 days for two weeks.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Grazing Diary. You chart and explain what you found.
flow.do: 1. Make a bar for each cut. 2. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Did the wheat grow back the same each time? Did cutting close to the soil make a difference?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each cut. Did they grow back the same each time? Why?
flow.parent: Most often the regrowth gets smaller after several cuts, and the plants cut at 1 centimetre slow down sooner. Young wheat lives on the seed's stored food and on the light their leaves catch, and each cut takes some away. Some plants may die. Whatever happens, it is a real result. This is overgrazing in a tub.

challenges.title: Save the Slope
challenges.problem: A bare tub of soil, tilted like a hillside, loses soil every time it rains. Without growing anything, find a way to keep the soil in the tub when you pour rain on it.
constraints: Use the same tilt and the same 2 cups of rain as in the Bare Tub Test.
Compare the runoff with a bare tub.
materials: the bare tub from the Bare Tub Test, refilled with soil
dry leaves, coir from a coconut, old cloth, ice-cream sticks, small stones
general: Cover the soil with dry leaves or coir. Farmers call this mulch. It softens the drops.
Push ice-cream sticks into the soil in rows across the slope, like little walls. Farmers on hills build steps called terraces.
Lay an old cloth or a coir mat over the soil and pin it down.
creative: Make small ridges of soil across the slope with your finger, like the contour bunds farmers build.
Put stones at the bottom edge to make a small check dam that slows the water.
Mix the ideas: terraces of sticks with leaves on each step.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to save the slope. Draw it, build it and rain on it. Is the runoff clearer than from the bare tub?

setup.art: A tilted tub of bare soil with brown water running off into a bowl.
setup.caption: 1. See the problem: the bare slope loses soil.

setup.art: A tilted tub of soil covered with dry leaves and rows of ice-cream sticks across the slope.
setup.caption: 2. Build a cover or walls.

setup.art: Two bowls side by side: one with brown runoff, one with much clearer water.
setup.caption: 3. Rain on it and compare the runoff.

flow.context: This is the first step of Save the Slope. You see the problem again.
flow.do: Refill the bare tub, tilt it, and rain 2 cups on it. Keep the bowl of runoff.
flow.say: This is what happens to a bare hillside. Now we keep the soil without growing anything.
flow.kid: Rain on the bare tub. Look at the brown water. That is soil leaving.

flow.context: This is the planning step of Save the Slope.
flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: Engineers draw first. What could soften the drops, or slow the water down?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas to keep the soil in the tub.

flow.context: This is the building and testing step of Save the Slope.
flow.do: 1. Refill the tub with fresh soil. 2. Build one idea. 3. Rain 2 cups on it. 4. Compare the runoff with the bare tub's bowl.
flow.say: Is this water clearer than the bare tub's? What did your idea do to the drops?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Rain on it. Is the water clearer?
flow.parent: Dry leaves or coir usually make the biggest difference, because they stop drops hitting the soil. Sticks alone help less unless they are close together.

flow.context: This is the last step of Save the Slope.
flow.do: Read the usual and creative ideas together, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here is what farmers do. Can you think of one more way?
flow.kid: Read the farmers' ideas. Can you invent a new one?
flow.think: A forest floor is covered in fallen leaves all year. What does that do in the monsoon?

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3 in Mysuru, cuts wheat and moong plants at 2 centimetres above the soil. Four days later, which will be taller?
items.why: Wheat grows from the bottom of each leaf, so the cut leaves keep pushing up. Moong grows from the tip of each stem, and the tips were cut off. Picking 'both the same' means thinking no plant can grow after cutting.

items.p: Using and protecting something carefully, so that it lasts, is called ____.
items.why: Conservation means taking care that soil, water, forests and animals last. A strong answer could add an example, such as picking a few curry leaves from each branch.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'When a cow eats grass, that grass plant is finished.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The cow bites off the top, but the growing point at the bottom of each leaf is left, so the grass grows again. A strong answer says where the grass grows from.

items.p: Match each animal to one thing she gives people.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these animals gives people something. A strong answer could also say one thing each animal needs in return.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Hyderabad, writes down what her family did on Sunday. Sort each one: does it save water or waste it?
items: brushing teeth with a mug of water
Saves water
leaving the tap running while soaping hands
Wastes water
watering the plants with rice-washing water
Saves water
a tap that drips all day
Wastes water
washing the car with a bucket, not a hose
Saves water
sending terrace rain into a pit
Saves water
items.a: see items
items.why: Using only what you need, using water twice, and helping rain soak into the ground all save water. A running tap or a drip lets clean water go down the drain.

items.p: Why can a cow eat the same field of grass every day without finishing it? Use the words 'growing point' in your answer.
items.a: A grass leaf's growing point is at the bottom, near the soil. The cow bites off the top and leaves the growing point, so the leaf keeps growing.
items.why: A strong answer says where the growing point is, and that the cow does not eat the growing point.

items.p: On a hot afternoon, a buffalo walks into a pond and lies there with only her head showing. Why?
opts: She heats up fast and is cooling down
items.why: A buffalo has dark skin and few sweat glands, so she gets hot quickly in the sun. Lying in water or mud, called wallowing, cools her. That is why buffaloes need a pond or a shower in summer.

items.p: Draw one cut wheat plant and one cut moong plant, four days after the Cutting Test. Mark with a dot where each plant grows from.
items.art: Two blank pots side by side with a soil line.
items.a: The wheat is taller, with flat leaf tips and a dot near the soil. The moong is a short stump, with the dot at the top of the stem, where the tip was cut off.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference in height and puts the growing point low for wheat and at the stem tip for moong.

items.p: Three of these plants are grasses, which grow from the bottom of their leaves. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Rice, sugarcane and bamboo are all grasses. A tomato plant grows from the tips of their stems, like moong.

items.p: In the Bare Tub Test, you rain the same water on a bare tub and a tub of wheat. What do you expect to see in the bowls?
opts: Browner water from the bare tub
Browner water from the wheat tub
items.why: On bare soil, the drops knock grains loose and the water carries them away. In the wheat tub, roots hold the soil and leaves soften the drops.

items.p: When heavy rain washes the top layer of soil off a bare field, this is called soil ____.
items.why: Soil erosion is soil carried away by water or wind. A strong answer could add that roots help stop it.

items.p: 1 millimetre of rain falling on 1 square metre of roof makes 1 litre of water.
items.why: True. A square metre covered with water 1 millimetre deep holds exactly 1 litre. So a big terrace catches a lot of water in one rain.

items.p: Two sisters in Coimbatore are looking after their grandmother's cows for a week.

views.says: Grass grows back, so we can keep the cows in the same small field all week.
We should move them to a new field every two days.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Use what you found in the Cutting Test. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer says grass does grow back, as Kavya says, but only so fast. If the cows eat a small field faster than it regrows, it turns bare. Moving them gives each field time to grow.
items.why: Both have part of it. Grass regrows, and the speed of regrowth decides how long animals can stay.

items.p: Put the steps of the Cutting Test in order.
items: Cut both kinds at 2 centimetres
Soak the wheat and moong overnight
Measure the plants for four days
Sow them in one tub and water them
a: Soak the wheat and moong overnight
Sow them in one tub and water them
Measure the plants for four days
items.why: First the seeds must grow, then you cut them like a cow grazing, then you watch what grows back.

items.p: Farhan's family ties their vegetable peels in a plastic bag and leaves it by the road. A cow comes by. What could happen?
opts: The cow may swallow the bag, which stays in her stomach
The cow will carry the bag to the bin
items.why: Cows often swallow the whole bag to get the food. Plastic cannot be digested, so it builds up in the stomach and makes the cow ill. A bin with a lid keeps food waste away from her.

items.p: Name two ways your family could save water at home. Say how each one helps.
items.a: Brushing with a mug instead of a running tap uses a little water, not litres. Fixing a dripping tap stops water being lost all day.
items.why: A strong answer gives real actions and says what each one saves.

items.p: Revathi says, 'To make grass grow back faster, cut it right down at the soil.' What is wrong with her idea?
items.a: The growing point of a grass leaf is at the bottom, near the soil. Cutting right at the soil can damage it, and leaves no green to make food. Grass grows back best when some leaf is left.
items.why: A strong answer uses where the growing point is, and why leaves are needed.

items.p: Why does a moong stem stop getting taller after its tip is cut off?
opts: Moong grows from the tip of the stem
items.why: Moong makes new stem at the tip, so cutting the tip takes away the growing part. A bud lower down may slowly grow a side shoot. Picking 'too wet' means looking for a cause that was the same for both plants.

items.p: Herders in Rajasthan walk their sheep and camels to new places through the year. Why does this help the land?
items.a: Each place gets time for the plants to grow back before the animals return, so no place is eaten bare.
items.why: A strong answer links moving to regrowth and to stopping overgrazing.

items.p: Good soil forms in just a few years.
items.why: False. Soil forms very slowly from broken rock and dead plants. A few centimetres can take hundreds of years, so lost soil is hard to replace.

items.p: A building in Chennai sends rain from its terrace into a pit of stones and sand. What does this refill?
items.why: The water soaks down through the pit into the ground, filling the gaps between sand and rock. Wells and borewells draw on this groundwater.

items.p: Three people talk about keeping cows for milk.

views.says: I know each of my cows by name, keep them cool and call the vet when they are ill.
Milk is made for the calf. We should not keep animals to take from them, however kindly.
Whatever people choose, we can check whether the animal is healthy, can move, rest and be with others.

items.ask: Which view is closest to yours? Give one reason. Then say one fair point another person makes.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason and fairly states a point from another view.
items.why: This is a real disagreement. Each person cares about the animals in a different way.

items.p: Draw a building with rainwater harvesting. Show the rain, the terrace, the pipe, the pit and the water going into the ground.
items.art: A blank outline of a two-storey building on a line of ground.
items.a: Rain on the terrace, a pipe down the side, a pit of stones and sand, and arrows from the pit down into the ground.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the whole path of the water, from the sky into the ground.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: to eat grass and low plants a little at a time
eating plants faster than they grow back
water that fills the gaps in soil and rock underground
to carry pollen from one flower to another
to lie in water or mud to cool down
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Why did Tamil Nadu make rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings in 2003?
opts: Roofs and roads stopped rain soaking in, and groundwater was falling
items.why: When the ground is covered by buildings and roads, rain runs into drains. Sending it into pits helps refill the groundwater.

items.p: A honeybee carries pollen from flower to flower while she drinks nectar. This helps the flowers make seeds and fruit. We say the bee ____ the flowers.
items.why: To pollinate is to carry pollen between flowers. Many crops, like mangoes and many vegetables, give more fruit when bees visit them.

items.p: Sort these plants by where they grow from.
cats: From the bottom of the leaf
From the tip of the stem
items: wheat
From the bottom of the leaf
rice
From the bottom of the leaf
spring onion
From the bottom of the leaf
moong
From the tip of the stem
bhindi
From the tip of the stem
tomato
From the tip of the stem
items.a: see items
items.why: Grasses and onions add new leaf from low down. Moong, bhindi and tomato grow at the tips of their stems, so a grazing animal does them more harm.

items.p: Write about your Bare Tub Test in three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why.
items.a: What I think: plant roots keep soil from washing away. What I saw: the bare tub's water was brown, with soil at the bottom, and the wheat tub's water was clearer. Why: roots hold the soil and leaves soften the drops.
items.why: A strong answer gives a claim, the evidence from the bowls, and a reason.

items.p: A silkworm caterpillar can live well on any kind of leaf.
items.why: False. Silkworms eat mulberry leaves and almost nothing else. Silk farmers grow mulberry fields to feed them.

items.p: In 1982, buffaloes were sent out of Keoladeo National Park, a wetland for birds in Rajasthan. What happened next?
opts: A tall wetland grass spread over the shallow water
The water dried up at once
items.why: The buffaloes had been eating the grass called Paspalum. Without them, it spread over the open water that many water birds use.

items.p: Put the journey of rain in a rainwater harvesting building in order.
items: The water soaks into the ground
Rain falls on the terrace
A borewell pumps it up later
A pipe carries it to a pit of stones and sand
a: A pipe carries it to a pit of stones and sand
The water soaks into the ground
A borewell pumps it up later
items.why: The rain is caught high up, led down, soaked into the ground, and used later.

items.p: Three of these protect soil from the rain. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Building steps called terraces on hills
items.why: A bare field has nothing to hold the soil or soften the drops, so the rain washes it away. The other three slow the water or cover the soil.

items.p: Selvi wants to test whether a cover of dry leaves stops soil washing away. Plan her fair test. What will she change, and what will she keep the same?
items.a: She changes only the cover: one tub with dry leaves, one bare. She keeps the same soil, the same tilt, the same amount of water, poured from the same height for the same time.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing and lists at least three things kept the same.

items.p: People argue about whether village buffaloes should graze inside Keoladeo National Park.

views.says: Buffaloes trample nests and eat food the wild animals need. Keep them out.
The wetland was shaped by grazing for centuries. A few buffaloes keep the grass down and the water open for birds.
Our buffaloes grazed here before it was a park. We need the grass for them.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one fair point from another view.
items.a: A strong answer uses what happened after 1982, when the grass spread, and also admits a fair point, such as nests being trampled or too many buffaloes harming the land.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. The number of animals, and how they are managed, matters.

items.p: Malini's family mows their lawn very short every two days in May. The lawn turns brown and thin. Why?
opts: The grass has too little leaf left to make food, and uses up its stores
Grass does not grow in May
The mower makes the grass cold
items.why: Grass needs leaves to catch sunlight and make food. Cut too often and too short, they use up the food stored in their roots. This is like overgrazing.

items.p: Why do you think grasses keep their growing points low, near the soil? Think about who eats grass.
items.a: Cows, goats, deer and insects eat grass all the time. A growing point near the soil is below where teeth bite, so the grass survives being eaten and grows again.
items.why: A strong answer links where the growing point is to the grass's own problem: being eaten often.

items.p: Kavya says, 'If something grows back, we can take it for ever.' Use the Grazing Diary to say whether she is right.
items.a: Only partly. The wheat grew back, but after several cuts it grew back less, especially when cut close to the soil. We can take for ever only if we take less than grows back.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from repeated cutting and says how much can be taken.

items.p: A family in Chennai has a terrace and gets about 1,400 millimetres of rain a year. Which is the best use of the terrace rain?
opts: Let it run into the street drain
Send it into a recharge pit, or store it in a tank
Cover the terrace so no rain falls
items.why: A pit puts the rain back into the ground, and a tank stores it for use. Rain sent to the drain is lost to the sea.

items.p: Draw a grass leaf just after it is cut, and the same leaf three days later. Use an arrow to show where the new part grew.
items.art: Two blank boxes labelled 'just cut' and '3 days later'.
items.a: The second leaf is taller, with the same flat tip, and an arrow at the bottom near the soil showing new leaf added there.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the flat cut tip and adds the new growth at the base.

items.p: The trees on a hillside in the Western Ghats are cut down. In the next monsoon, what will the stream at the bottom of the hill look like?
opts: Muddier, carrying soil from the bare slope
items.why: Without roots and fallen leaves, the rain washes soil off the slope into the stream. That is soil erosion, and the stream turns brown.

items.p: A honeybee that drinks from a flower sprayed with poison can be harmed.
items.why: True. Many insect poisons sprayed on crops also harm bees. That is why bees need flowers that have not been sprayed.

items.p: It is May in Chennai. Plan how your family could help the street dogs near your building. Give three things they need and why.
items.a: Fresh water in a shady bowl, changed every day, because dogs can't sweat much and May is very hot. Shade to rest in. A rabies vaccine, through the local animal welfare group, so they stay healthy.
items.why: A strong answer gives real needs, each with a reason.

items.p: Sort these by how fast they come back once used.
cats: Comes back in weeks or a few years
Takes hundreds of years or more
items: grass in a field
Comes back in weeks or a few years
curry leaves on a plant
Comes back in weeks or a few years
fish in the sea, if the fishing stops for a season
Comes back in weeks or a few years
a few centimetres of good soil
Takes hundreds of years or more
very deep, old groundwater
Takes hundreds of years or more
a 500-year-old banyan tree
Takes hundreds of years or more
items.a: see items
items.why: Conservation means knowing how fast something comes back, and taking less than that. Slow things must be used very carefully.

items.p: In 2019, the main lakes that supply Chennai went almost dry. How did the city get water?
opts: From trains and tankers bringing water from elsewhere
items.why: Water was brought in by train and by tanker lorries. The crisis showed how much the city depends on rain being saved.

items.p: Put these in order to show how overgrazing ruins a field.
items: The rain washes the bare soil away
Too many goats are kept in one field
The roots die
The plants are eaten down to the ground
a: Too many goats are kept in one field
The plants are eaten down to the ground
The rain washes the bare soil away
items.why: Each step causes the next. Once the soil is gone, it takes hundreds of years to form again.

items.p: Ravi says, 'The water from the wheat tub was clearer because the wheat drank all the rain.' Find the mistake in his thinking.
items.a: Water still ran out of the wheat tub, so the wheat did not drink it all. It was clearer because the roots held the soil and the leaves softened the drops.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence that water came out of both tubs.

items.p: Water that soaks deep into the ground, which wells and borewells pump up, is called ____.
items.why: Groundwater fills the tiny spaces between grains of soil, sand and rock. Rain refills it, if the rain can soak in.

items.p: Match each place or movement to its state.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are places in this unit where people protected forests, wetlands and animals.

quiz.why: Silk is the thread a silkworm caterpillar spins to make her cocoon. Bees give honey, and sheep give wool.

quiz.p: Anu cuts the top off her lawn grass and the top off her tulsi plant. Which grows taller again from the same stem or leaf?
quiz.why: Grass grows from the bottom of the leaf, so the cut leaf keeps growing. Tulsi grows from the tips of their stems, so they make new side shoots instead.

opts: Animals eating plants faster than they grow back
Animals eating only the tops of grass
quiz.why: Overgrazing leaves the ground bare. Eating only the tops, slowly, lets grass grow back.

quiz.p: In the Cutting Test, why do we measure 3 wheat plants and not just 1?
quiz.why: One plant might be weak or damaged. Measuring three shows what most plants do.

opts: Picking a few curry leaves from each branch, so the plant grows more
Cutting the whole curry leaf plant at once
Pulling the plant out by the roots
quiz.why: Conservation is taking in a way that lets the plant keep growing. Taking everything leaves nothing to grow back.

quiz.p: Arjun brushes his teeth with the tap running. His sister Priya uses a mug of water. Who uses less water?
quiz.why: A running tap pours litres while you brush. A mug holds about a quarter of a litre.

quiz.p: Why did a wetland grass spread over the water at Keoladeo after 1982?
opts: The buffaloes that ate it were sent out
quiz.why: The buffaloes had kept the grass short. Without them, it grew over the open water.

quiz.p: Why does soil under grass wash away less than bare soil?
opts: Roots hold it, and leaves soften the drops
quiz.why: Roots grip the soil grains, and leaves stop the drops hitting the soil hard.

quiz.p: What does a hen need to stay healthy?
quiz.why: Damp and dirt bring disease to hens. Ponds are for buffaloes, and mulberry leaves are for silkworms.

quiz.p: In a city, why does less rain soak into the ground?
opts: Roads and buildings cover the soil
City soil is full of water
quiz.why: Rain runs off roads and roofs into drains. Rainwater harvesting sends it back into the ground.

quiz.p: What does India's Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act of 1960 do?
opts: Makes it a crime to beat, starve or neglect an animal
quiz.why: The law protects animals from cruelty. People may keep animals, but must care for them.

quiz.p: In the Bare Tub Test, what must be the same for both tubs?
opts: The soil, the tilt and the amount of water
quiz.why: Only the cover should differ. Then any difference in the runoff comes from the roots.

quiz.p: Where is the growing point of a grass leaf?
opts: At the bottom, near the soil
quiz.why: The new leaf is made at the bottom and pushes up. That is why the cut tips stay flat as the leaf grows.

applications: Lawns, playgrounds and cricket grounds can be mowed every week because grass grows from the base.
Herders and dairy farmers move animals between fields so the grass can grow back.
Farmers cover soil with crop stubble, leaves or a cover crop so the monsoon does not wash it away.
Tea and coffee estates on hills plant along the slopes and keep the ground covered.
Buildings in Tamil Nadu and many other states must harvest rainwater.
Fishing stops for some weeks each year on India's coasts, so fish can breed.
Vets, animal shelters and animal welfare groups care for working and street animals.
Beekeepers place hives near crops like mustard and sunflower, so the bees pollinate them.
Silk farmers in Karnataka grow mulberry fields to feed their silkworms.

open_questions.q: How many animals can a field or a hill feed for ever without being harmed?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on the rain, the soil, the plants and the animals, and it changes from year to year. Scientists still argue about how to measure it.

open_questions.q: Did grasses and grazing animals shape each other?
open_questions.why_open: Grasses and grazers spread together over millions of years. How much each one changed the other is still being studied from fossils of teeth and plants.

open_questions.q: How much does rainwater harvesting really refill a city's groundwater?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies in Chennai found well levels rising after 2003, but many pits are not cleaned, and the amount is hard to measure across a whole city.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to protect a wild place: keep people and their animals out, or let them share it carefully?
open_questions.why_open: Keoladeo and other places show both ways can go wrong. The answer may be different for every place.

maths.problem: In the Cutting Test, a wheat plant was cut at 2 centimetres. Four days later it was 7 centimetres tall. How much did it grow in the four days, and how much is that each day?
maths.answer: 5 centimetres in four days, which is about 1 and a quarter centimetres each day.
maths.explain: 7 take away 2 is 5, so it grew 5 centimetres. 5 shared over 4 days is 1 centimetre each day, with 1 centimetre left over, shared as a quarter each day.
maths.context: This is about the Cutting Test, where you cut wheat and moong at 2 centimetres and measure what grows back.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the starting height tells us how much really grew, not just how tall the plant is.

maths.problem: Rain falls 10 millimetres deep on a terrace of 50 square metres. How many litres of water fell on the terrace?
maths.explain: 1 millimetre on 1 square metre is 1 litre. 10 millimetres on 1 square metre is 10 litres. On 50 square metres it is 50 times 10, which is 500 litres.
maths.context: This is about the Rain Gauge, where you measure how much rain falls on your home.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the depth by the area turns a few millimetres in a bottle into the water that falls on a whole roof.

maths.problem: A dripping tap fills 40 millilitres in 10 minutes. How much does it waste in one hour?
maths.explain: An hour is 60 minutes, which is 6 groups of 10 minutes. 6 times 40 is 240 millilitres.
maths.context: This is about the Drip Count, where you catch the water from a dripping tap.
maths.why_maths: A tiny drip looks like nothing, but multiplying shows how much it adds up to.

maths.problem: In the Four Fields game, a field has 5 tokens. Each round the herd eats 2 and the field grows 1 back. After how many rounds is it down to 2 tokens? What happens if the herd stays longer?
maths.answer: After 3 rounds. If the herd stays, the field soon reaches 0 and turns bare.
maths.explain: Each round the field loses 2 and gains 1, so it loses 1 overall. 5, then 4, then 3, then 2. Staying on means 1, then 0.
maths.context: This is about Four Fields, a game where you move a herd between fields so the grass can grow back.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern, minus 1 each round, lets a herder predict when a field will run out before it happens.

maths.problem: Tamil Nadu made rainwater harvesting compulsory in 2003. Chennai's lakes went almost dry in 2019. How many years apart are these?
maths.explain: 2019 take away 2003. 2003 plus 10 is 2013, and 6 more is 2019. So it is 16 years.
maths.context: This is about the card on saving water and putting rain back into the ground.
maths.why_maths: Working out the gap between dates helps us see how long a change has had to work.

roots.context: We have learned how grass grows back, what useful animals need, and how soil and water are kept. Now we ask what this tells us about taking from the world.

deep_truth.truth: In your tub, the cut wheat grew back within days, and the cut moong stems stayed short. Both lost the same height. Wheat keeps their growing point low, below the cut, and moong keeps theirs at the tip. So taking from a living thing can go on only if the part that grows is left behind.
deep_truth.habit: We think taking always uses something up, like cutting a whole bunch of coriander. But the wheat lost as much as the moong and kept growing. What decides is not how much is taken, but whether the growing part is left.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Cutting Test, the cut wheat grew several centimetres in four days, with their flat cut tips pushed up from below. The moong stumps did not grow taller. In the Grazing Diary, wheat cut close to the soil again and again grew back less each time.

three.who_am_i: Your hair and nails also grow from the bottom, so cutting the ends does not stop them.
three.what_is_life: Grass and grazing animals have lived together for millions of years. The grass feeds the cow, and the cow's dung feeds the soil the grass grows in.
three.what_is_this_world: The same rain falls on the field, soaks into the ground and comes back up in a well. The water we save today is the water someone drinks later.

roots.thread: One grass seed becomes a plant, and that plant feeds cows, goats, grasshoppers and the soil below. The cow's milk feeds a family, and her dung goes back to the field. Each of these lives is separate, and each depends on the grass keeping their growing point low. Where people take only the top, the field keeps feeding all of them. One plant's way of growing holds up many lives.

teachings.teaching: All this world is filled by the One. Enjoy it by letting go. Do not grab what belongs to others.
teachings.link: The cow eats only the top and lets the rest go, so the field lasts. Taking with a light hand is what keeps the growing part alive.

teachings.teaching: Without water, the world cannot go on.
teachings.link: Every animal on the farm, every field and every city depends on rain. Saving water and sending rain back into the ground keeps the world going.

science.text: Grass leaves grow from a growing point near their base, so grazing and mowing remove old leaf, not the part that makes new leaf.
How many animals a piece of land can feed for ever depends on rain, soil and plants, and is still argued about for each place.

other_view.view: Grass keeps their growing point low because, over millions of years, the grasses that did so survived grazing best. It is how they adapted, not a gift to the cow. Reading lessons about taking and giving into it says more about us than about grass.

how_we_found_out.story: Keoladeo, near Bharatpur in Rajasthan, is a shallow wetland where thousands of water birds spend the winter, including painted storks, herons and, in the past, rare Siberian cranes. For hundreds of years, buffaloes from nearby villages grazed there. Many people, including scientists of the Bombay Natural History Society such as the bird expert Salim Ali, thought the buffaloes harmed the birds by eating their food and trampling the wetland. Keoladeo became a national park in 1981, and grazing was banned in 1982. Then something unexpected happened. A wetland grass called Paspalum, which the buffaloes used to eat, spread across the shallow water. It made thick mats where open water had been, and birds that feed in open water lost space. Park staff had to cut the grass by hand. Scientists of the same society studied the park for years. Their report in 1991 said that grazing had been keeping the wetland open, and suggested letting some grazing back. The wrong idea was that a wild place is always best protected by keeping its animals out.
how_we_found_out.who: Scientists of the Bombay Natural History Society, including Salim Ali, who first supported the ban, and the team whose long study came out in 1991
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the buffaloes only harmed the wetland, so keeping them out would help the birds. Instead, the grass they had been eating spread over the open water, and the long study showed that some grazing had kept the wetland healthy.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Whole wheat sprouts reliably within 2 to 3 days in a warm room and reaches 8 to 12 centimetres in about a week, so the cut comes on day 9. In a cold room the steps say to wait longer. Moong seed leaves sit low, so the cut step says to cut below them, so the stump has no leaves left. The Bare Tub Test needs a separate tub of wheat sown on the same day, because the Cutting Test tub is half moong. The rain bottle needs holes made by a grown-up, and the test is done in the bathroom. The Onion Test uses spring onions from any vegetable shop and shows new green in 2 or 3 days. The Drip Count reuses the water for plants. The Rain Gauge depends on a rainy day, so it is not in the spine, and it gives a city rainfall figure to use instead. Both games work for one child alone. The spine fits about 85 minutes, with the Cutting Test spread over 13 days in short daily visits.
